utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are continuing with the Prosecution. I see we have a new witness. Can the witness please make the solemn declaration. Can she stand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Bobic. Could I ask you just to state your date and place of birth for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: My name is Ediba Bobic. I was born on the 31st of October, 1950, in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you -- you were born in Brcko. Did you later move to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: It was on the 1st of May, 1998 or 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic --

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: In 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you mean 1998 or 1968, Mrs. Bobic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise. It was in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you're married to Mr. Kemal Bobic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you have children in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, two sons.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And could you tell the Chamber what you were working as in Bosanski Samac, and if you and your husband and your family owned any businesses in Bosanski Samac after you moved there?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. My husband and I had a catering facility and a hamburger stand which we operated up until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you used to work in this hamburger stand; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were making kebabs there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was the name of this place you worked in Sedrvan?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. This catering facility, cafe, was called Sedrvan. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And I understand that where you lived in Bosanski Samac you also had two businesses under your house, a little shop and a herb pharmacy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think perhaps the microphone could be moved closer to the witness. Maybe all her answers are not being picked up.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, I'd like to ask you about some people who were in Bosanski Samac and ask you whether you know them. Do you know a gentleman by the name of Mr. Miroslav Tadic? Mrs. Bobic, could I ask you to speak a bit louder for the record so that the translators can hear your answers.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So perhaps you could just let the Chamber know whether or not you do in fact know a gentleman by the name of Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how did you know Mr. Tadic? Did you know him well? Did you know him in a social context?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Tadic very well. I know him from the school. He used to work as a teacher, and occasionally he would come to our cafe, have breakfast there, coffee, so we knew him well. Later on he opened up a cafe himself, and occasionally we would visit his cafe, but once the Cafe AS became a gambling place as well, we did not go there any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, could I ask you to have a look around the Chamber this morning and see if you see the Miroslav Tadic you've described to the Chamber; and if you can see him, could you describe where he's sitting for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miroslav is sitting on the first chair, I think to the left. He has a moustache, glasses; he's writing down something.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can the record reflect that Mr. Tadic has been identified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, do you also know someone called Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And could you also explain to the Chamber the context you know Mr. Zaric in and how well you know him.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric came to Bosanski Samac approximately a year after me, and he married Fatima, and he lived with her up until the war. We lived in the same neighbourhood. He worked at the SUP and occasionally would come to our restaurant, eat kebabs there. Sometimes we would sit together. Occasionally we would celebrate birthdays together. But bad times came afterwards, such bad times that we had to leave our town.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Mrs. Bobic, could you also see if you could identify Mr. Simo Zaric in this Chamber today, and if so, to describe for the record who you identify as Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric is sitting in the middle of the desk, next to Miro Brko. I know him well. He knows me well as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the record can reflect that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Mrs. Bobic, the third gentleman, Mr. Blagoje Simic, do you know Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And could you explain to us again how well you know Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I have known Blagoje since he was a student. He used to come to our place, and we used to see him as a doctor. He was our treating physician. He treated us, respected us. But, however, the bad times came afterwards and we were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And as you've done with the other two, could you please see if you could identify Blagoje Simic is here today; and if you do see the Blagoje Simic you're talking about, for the record, tell us where you see him.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic is sitting in the first chair to my right or to my left -- well, if I were to stand in front, then I guess it would be to my left. He has a short beard. He has changed a bit from the time when he was younger, but however I know him well, so I can recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I -- the record reflect that Mr. Simic has been identified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, I'd like to ask you some questions about Bosanski Samac in around the time period 1991 and 1992. Had you heard of an organisation called the 4th Detachment at this time period in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And what did you know of the 4th Detachment prior to the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: All I knew was that that was some kind of a military organisation preparing some kind of a defence against Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did you know whether any of the defendants that you've identified this morning were involved with the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I think that all three were involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, I need to ask you just one or two questions about a topic I don't intend to dwell on, but just for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Reidy. I wonder whether you can clarify. The witness said that she thinks that all three were involved. Does she think other? Does she know?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, perhaps you could clarify that for us. I'll take you through each defendant. Mr. Simo Zaric, do you have any knowledge as to whether or not he was involved with the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric recruited young people and everybody else for his 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And do you know this -- how do you know this information that he was recruiting people?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: This is something that he should know as well. We lived in the same neighbourhood. We saw everything that was happening. We knew everything. They started distancing themselves from us. They wouldn't come to our restaurants any more. They simply distanced themselves from us. They started gathering at Miro Brko's cafes [As interpreted]. Personnel carriers would come there frequently, and I would see them in his presence. Because I had to pass by his cafe on my way to my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, when you say "they started distancing themselves," could you just clarify for the record who you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an objection concerning to interpretation, page 6, line 24, the witness said they used to gather in the cafe of Miro Brko's brother and that is not what is reflected in the transcript. We heard the witness say that they used to gather in the cafe of Miro Brko's brother. So could we clarify that.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. That cafe was close to my house, the cafe belonging to Miro Brko's brother. Personnel carriers would be there and various troops. The brother of Miro Brko was also known to distribute Malboro cigarettes to his troops that were moving in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Miro's brother, this is a man called Vlajko Tadic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So now Mr. Miroslav Tadic himself, do you have any information as to whether he was connected with the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And what makes you so certain?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, because he was involved in the exchange of many people.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So prior to the takeover on the 17th of April, 1992, did you have reason to believe that Miroslav Tadic was a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We did not have a reason to suppose so, but this is how it was. We were all surprised by this.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say you were surprised, what do you mean that you were surprised? In what way were you surprised?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I was surprised because he used to teach our children, educate them, and then later on some bad things happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, Mr. Blagoje Simic. Did you have any -- do you have any knowledge as to whether or not he was involved with the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I think that we saw him at the municipal building as the president of the municipal government, that at that time he was already involved in those Serbian organisations, that he was together with the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, are you now talking about the period before the 17th of April, 1992, or after the takeover of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: After the takeover of power in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So for the moment I'd like to continue to concentrate on the time before the 17th of April, 1992, and at that time do you have any information as to whether Blagoje Simic was involved with the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, Dr. Simic did not want to attend any meetings that were public except those that were the meetings of the Chetnik organisations. This is how it was before the 17th. We knew that he was there with his people.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say "Chetnik organisations," what organisations specifically are you referring to or do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, you said you had two sons. One of them was -- your eldest son was called Enver; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And is it correct that he was tragically killed in an explosion on the 14th of February, just before the war?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And I understand that after that time you were in mourning and you weren't paying much attention to what was happening in Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'd like just to ask you now about the 16th of April, 1992. Were you at home with your family on the night of the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And at some stage during that night were you awakened by the sounds of gunfire or shooting?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: At that moment, we heard somebody walking in my yard. I got up, turned on the light, looked through the window, and I heard somebody say, "Turn off the light or I will shoot." I didn't see who it was, and I didn't know at the time what was going on. After that, we heard an explosion from the direction of the SUP building. We all became quiet. We didn't leave the house. We remained like that until 5.00 a.m. The dawn started breaking out. I opened the door and came out, and there was nobody in the street. There was nothing going on. We remained in the stairwell really quiet.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Is your house located near to the SUP and the Territorial Defence buildings?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that --

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: My house -- my house is located in Lola Ribar Street. There was just one passage between the houses -- in between my house and the main street. This is where the troops used to pass. I suppose they were on their way to the TO building. They were jumping over the fences in order to get to the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So is it that the back of your house, the yard of your house, backs on to the street where the TO and the SUP buildings are? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. Between our house and my yard, there is another house, and only after that you get to the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was it your impression that people were passing through your yard that evening to get to the SUP and TO buildings?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the conclusion we made that same day upon hearing that Samac had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said that you remained very quiet until about 5.00 in the morning. What happened then at 5.00 in the morning? Did you go outside to have a look at what was going on?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. I just opened the door and looked at the road. There was nobody there. Everything was empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how did you first receive information that there had been a takeover in Bosanski Samac that evening?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: My husband had friends, and two of them called me. One was Vlado Sarkanovic and Djordje Pisarevic, called Ruka. They called us and told us that Samac had fallen and wondered what we're going to do, because Samac fell into Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you recall exactly what they had said to you? When they said it had fallen, what exactly did they mean by that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, they meant that since we were Muslims, we would have no rights there any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did they tell you who was now in charge of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: He said the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you hear any other public --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise to my learned colleague, but I didn't react first time, then it was the second time. This is actually the second time that I have noticed that our learned colleague from the Prosecution is calling a witness to speculate. First time it was what was her impression regarding the soldiers, and it was the way that they went jumping through fences and things like that. But this was actually the second time, what was actually her impression and what -- the words that Mr. Sarkanovic and Mr. Djordje Pisarevic said to her, what they meant. Actually, it was typical example of calling for speculation what someone else meant. And I would just like to ask my learned colleague to avoid these kinds of questions. This is a fact witness and it is not -- I don't believe that this is a witness who is -- well, speculation are important for this case. This is not an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Sometimes it's correct to ask a witness what they meant, because you're asking the witness what the witness understood by whatever was said to that witness. So, Ms. Reidy --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be careful the way I phrase it, but that's exactly what I meant. I think these are fact questions. I'm asking this witness to clarify exactly what was understood or what was heard, if I think there's an ambiguity on the record. I'm not intending to ask the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, did you receive -- or did you hear any other public announcements that morning or during the day about what had happened in Bosanski Samac or instructions about action you should take or how you should behave?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: During the first days, we realised we were unable to go outside. They started looking for weapons, and if somebody happened to have weapons, they came to our house, 15 of men, and told us we had to surrender the weapons that we did not have. My husband's brother, Faruk Bobic, was a hunter and died before the war. He had a trophy rifle, and they confiscated it and took it away. On that same day -- or rather, the following morning and afternoon, young guys started collecting people and things to protect facilities from shelling. They used to get sandbags and protect those facilities where people from the 4th Detachment were. It was very difficult for us. When going into the street, we were unable to approach anybody. People were afraid to greet each other because we were not allowed to gather in a group of more than three people. If we went to do our work obligation, we had to put a white armband in order to be able to go and work. It was very difficult for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bobic. I'd just like to ask you some more questions about some of the information you've given us, okay? The first thing I'd like to ask you more questions about is the men who came to take away weapons from your house. You said there were 10 or 15 of them. Did you know any of the people who came to take weapons?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was Tubonja there, Dragan Tubonja, Mersad Seric [As interpreted]. They had masks on, so I couldn't tell you who they were. It was just terrible, terrible to look, because after so many handsome faces that we used to see before, all of a sudden we would have these masked people coming to our door with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one clarification for the transcript. It's page 13, line 11. Here it said Mersad Seric. It was actually Naser Sejdic. This is what the witness said. Maybe just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy. You can correct the --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think my learned friend is correct. I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, you mentioned two people you recognised: Dragan Tubonja, and the second, was it Naser Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Naser Sejdic, a former policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said they had masks on. How did you recognise these two people? How do you know that these two were amongst the 15 or so people?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: They did not have painted faces. They were in ordinary clothes and they came to search my house. They searched it thoroughly from basement to the attic. They opened all closets. They threw things around. I don't know what they were looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So these men came with others who were wearing masks; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were these men in military uniform? Were they wearing a uniform, and if so, could you describe what sort of uniform, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in uniforms. Some people wore uniforms from the former army and some people wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were they all armed, carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I believe, then, that you said you received instructions that you were not to gather in groups of more than three is that correct? And do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, could I ask you just to speak a little louder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Could the chair be pushed forward? I think the witness is sitting too far from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, I need to ask you the question again for the record. Did you receive instructions that you could not gather in more than -- in groups of more than three?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how did you receive these instructions? Do you recall how you were told?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, it was broadcast over the radio, and when you got out, they simply pushed -- chased you away. They prevented you from meeting other people, and there were little pieces of paper posted around.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "they prevented you from meeting other people," who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: These were the men in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: They are people in camouflage uniform or police uniform, or both?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And I think you also said you received instructions that you had to wear white armbands. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how did you receive that information? Was it also over the radio?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Over the radio, and all the lads that went to work the first day had to tie the armbands, and they told us that if we went out, we had to wear the armbands to show that we were Muslims. It was most certainly done in order for them to be easier to round us up and to send us all into camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. After the first few days, were you -- did you receive instructions that you should leave your home and move into another place of shelter?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We were at our home. Vlajko came to our house and Vlajko is a neighbour of mine, and he said that we had to go and seek shelter in Idriz Nogic's house. And he gathered the entire street, from the first street leading to the SUP building down to Djakici, from the memorial home onwards. We all had to go to that shelter. I don't know why. He didn't explain why, but we had to leave our homes and go and find accommodation there. In this house where we were accommodated, this was not meant to accommodate people. This was a hen house. This was in an area where hens that were raised there were kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Bobic. You mentioned, a few minutes ago, that apart from broadcasts over the radio concerning the white armbands, that there were, in your words, "little pieces of paper posted around." I wonder whether you could just tell us a little bit more about those little pieces of paper, what they said, whether they were signed by somebody. Was there any indication on those little pieces of paper as to who was authorising the wearing of the white armbands?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- I don't have the transcript in front of me. I think, just from my recollection, was the bits of paper referring to the gathering in three or more and not the armbands? Just so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, yes, you're quite correct. Yes. The radio was the white armbands. You're quite correct, Ms. Reidy. The radio and the little pieces of paper were concerning the gathering in groups of three or more. But I'd still like to know something about those little pieces of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I understand. Just so the witness isn't confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you about the papers. They were posted on the trees, and it was stated there that more than two or three people could not gather and that we were not allowed to talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said two or three people. Did it say --

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Any people or did it refer to any specific ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Not even Serbs or Croats could gather in groups more than two or three people.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: These little pieces of paper -- the signs you saw on trees, when were you able to see these announcements on the trees?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: From the 14th February onwards, I didn't know the exact dates of any events, and -- because for me, the war started on the 14th of February. From then onwards, everything that I had was ruined for me. So I also learned about the date when the war ended, only later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, I understand that the tragic death of your son on the 14th of February is difficult for you, but I need to ask you if you can try to focus as much as you can on the time period I'm asking you about. Did you start forced labour, doing forced labour, later on, in the second half of 1992, a few months after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were on your way to report for forced labour, was that when you saw these announcements you said were put on trees?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: I read them, but I wouldn't be able to tell you the specific date. I'm really sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's okay. You said you read them -- Her Honour Judge Williams had asked whether you have any recollection as to if they were signed by anybody in particular or had any stamp on them. Do you have any recollection about that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I remember only that there was this piece of paper which was written on a computer, stating that we were not allowed to gather. We were not even allowed to gather around the tree to read this piece of paper. I was really exhausted at that time. I have to tell you that I had 43 kilos when I was released from the camp, and before the war I weighed a hundred kilos.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, you have told us that you were moved from your home and you mentioned the name of Vlajko. Is this -- Vlajko came to tell you to move. Is this Vlajko Tadic, the gentleman you've already mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: When Vlajko told us that we had to move out, we had to do so and go to Idriz's house. There were quite a few of us there. All of us from the street had to find accommodation there. The accommodation was very bad [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And is the -- the Vlajko, is that Vlajko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the house you were to move to, was that belonging to the gentleman Idriz Nogic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, could I ask you to repeated the answer, because it's not being picked up on the -- by the microphone.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a little correction to the interpretation. Page 18, 22, line 22. The word "shelter" is not contained in the transcript. The witness said "the accommodation in the shelter was very bad," and not that "the accommodation was very bad."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, perhaps you can correct that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, I don't know if you recall. You told us that you all had to find accommodation in Idriz's house. Did you say the accommodation was very bad or the accommodation in the shelter was very bad?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: The accommodation where we were. That was not a shelter. This was a place where a man had chickens. This is where we were. They called it a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said a lot of you were gathered there. Could you tell me the ethnicity of the people who were required to gather in this hen house?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats were gathered there. In fact, there was only one Croat woman in our street. Her name was Kadica. There was Idriz Nogic, with his wife, Gordana, who was a Serb. My entire family was also there, my sister, with her children, the Nogics, Emina, her mother, her brother. There was also Sadeta Kapetanovic, Arifa.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Apart from Mr. Nogic's wife, Gordana, were there any other Serb families required to gather in the house or were you all Muslim and Croats?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: No, there were no -- no, there were no Serb families; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any choice in moving to this accommodation?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We had no choice. We had to go there, as they had told us. Why would I have left my house otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You didn't want to leave your house?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were all gathered there, did people come by to check on you?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vlajko Tadic came. It seems that he was in charge of our street.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when he came by to check, would he say anything in particular, or what did he do when he came by to check?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: When he came by, he said that we were not to go out, that we had to stay in.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained there, were any of the men arrested from Mr. Idriz Nogic's?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How many men were arrested, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Two, as far as I know. That's correct. There was Batan and Suma. Batan's real name was Sead Hurtic, and Suma's real name was -- just a minute. Ruzmir Hodzic. Ruzmir or Rusmir.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall who carried out those arrests?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them. They simply got out and never came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So was it the others in the accommodation with you who told you they had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: The others said that they had been taken away to the TO, but we heard that on that very same day, Batan was killed, and Ruzmir was beaten quite badly and then he was taken to hospital, where he stayed for a long time, and later on that's where he died.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Apart from the men that were arrested, were any of the people gathered in the accommodation required to perform forced labour whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was your son, your second son is called Bedrudin. Was he required to do forced labour?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He went to gather sandbags, and so did Nermin Bobic, my sister's son, Milka Nogic [As interpreted] also went, and so did Emina.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How did your son and --

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Her name is not Milka, but Emina.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How did your son and your nephew and the others learn that they were required to perform forced labour, such as gathering sandbags?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: Lads would come with pieces of paper and asking people to go according to the list. We didn't know where they went, but when they came back, they would tell us what they had been doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The people who came with these lists, were they in uniform? Were they carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Right from the start, these were lads in uniforms that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You didn't know them yourself. Could you tell whether they were local people or non-locals, or did you not know?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell who they were, because I couldn't go out to look at them. But at any rate, young men went to work. They didn't want to do so, but they were forced to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your son, you said, had to gather sandbags. Was that the only task he was required to perform or was he required to perform other tasks as well?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. That's what they did at the beginning of the work obligation. Later on they had to do more difficult tasks, and they had to dig trenches and also requisition other people's property. So that would be harder work.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did your son, Bedrudin, ever receive any payment for these tasks that he would perform?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst your son was performing these tasks, do you know whether he was under armed guard?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How do you know that he was under armed guard?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Every time he came back in the evening, he would always tell me about his day.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was there ever any occasion that he was fired on whilst performing these tasks?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was this a frequent occurrence or did this happen just once or twice?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: My son was fired on once. He went to dig trenches during the night. It was the night shift. They were led by Mile, nicknamed Pancir. Right now I couldn't recall the last name of that man, because I find it hard to concentrate right now. He fired at his feet. He fell down and was brought home at around 3.30 a.m. in a very difficult condition. He didn't know what was going on. He was unconscious. I looked at him. He had high blood pressure and he was sweating. These were really very hard times for me. I don't know what to tell you. In the morning I gathered all my strength and went to the health care centre. Some doctors worked there who help me, really, so -- and he had really high blood pressure, 225. That's not something that a man can survive. We brought him home and he -- and left him lying there, and then after a while --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bobic. Don't worry. That's more than enough information. Perhaps you'd just like to take a minute or two before I ask you any more questions. Mrs. Bobic, if it's okay, I'd like to ask you some more questions. Did Behrudin perform forced labour all the time whilst -- every day whilst you were in Bosanski Samac after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Every day until the day of the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this initial period of the takeover as well, did you receive a distribution of some milk and bread?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. My neighbour Vlajko was in this group, he and his son Dragan. Vlajko Tadic and his son Dragan. They distributed bread on behalf of Bosanski Samac, I'm sure, and they gave bread and milk to everybody from our street.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this distribution happen once or did it happen on more occasions?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I know of only one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at some stage return to your own accommodation from that of Mr. Nogic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We came back without asking. Nobody told us to go back, but we simply went back because we didn't like where we were staying. So we went back to our house and took shelter below the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you recall roughly how long you may have stayed in Idriz Nogic's house? Was it a few weeks after the takeover? Mrs. Bobic, could you just maybe speak a little bit louder so that the microphone can get your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: We just want to get all your evidence. So could you tell me again, if you recall, how long you stayed in Idriz Nogic's?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: For a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it a matter of weeks?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We definitely stayed there several weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you moved back to your own accommodation, was your husband arrested?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. At that time he was at home. They came to arrest him on one occasion, with a white TAM truck, small truck. They banged on the door. I opened the door and in front of it I saw my neighbour, Fadil Topcagic, with another two men. The man who had a red beret recognised me right away. He asked me where Kemal was, and I told him that Kemal was inside. That man said that Fadil Topcagic could not take my husband because he would remain in our house --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The last phrase that the witness said was not clear.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: That man used to play chess with my husband. He was from Vukovar. He was not from Samac. And at the time when he played chess with my husband, he was not with Fadil Topcagic. There was a chess tournament, and they were unable to accommodate all the people that came to the tournament, so we put up some people in our house, and they stayed in our house. However, the war broke out, and after the war broke out this man came to our door, not knowing whom he was supposed to arrest. His name was Mile Kitic, called Vukovarac, and he said, "You will not take Kemal out of here," and he told Fadil to go on. Fadil went away. He came into our house, and on that occasion he saved my husband from being executed in Crkvina. So that day was very difficult, very tense for us. It was difficult to live through all that. Those moments were unexpected.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that you were -- two people came to arrest Kemal. One was Fadil Topcagic, another man you knew from before the war. Was he dressed in camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Fadil was not arrested that day, and through the intervention of a man --

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Not Fadil.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry. Kemal was not arrested that day. Thank you. Was he arrested afterwards?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Fadil came to get him.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: This is Fadil Topcagic? Did he come by himself or did he come in the company of other persons?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I just told you: Fadil was with Pero Kitic and another man. I can't tell you his name right away. I feel so tense that I can't remember the name right now. There were three other men in that van in which they came to arrest Kemal. They put rifles out right away, but Kitic said that they wouldn't take him away. That was on the first occasion when they came to arrest him.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second occasion -- I understand on the second occasion Kemal was actually arrested, and I'd like to concentrate now on that second occasion.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was Kemal arrested from your home? Could you just - sorry - repeat your answer again? We're finding it hard to pick up. Was Kemal arrested from your home?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you recall who came to conduct the arrest?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Naser Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was Naser Sejdic by himself or was he accompanied by other persons?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: There were two other men with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were these men wearing any uniform and were they carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had uniforms and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were these camouflage uniforms or police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: All three were military uniforms. Naser wore a policeman's uniform, and the other two wore a military one.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they explain to Kemal or to you where they were taking him or for what reason they had come to take him away?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: Naser said that Kemal needed to go to have an informative interview. He left and did not come back until the 6th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was Kemal taken to the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know it's 20 minutes to our break, but I wonder if we can take a five-minute earlier break and perhaps the witness can take some time and compose herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can take an early break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall have a break of 20 minutes and resume the proceedings at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, before the break I -- you were giving your evidence about the arrest of your husband Kemal, and I asked you whether Kemal was taken to the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, Kemal was taken to the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you ever try to go to see him in the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I had to go to the SUP building because I was asked to report there in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And who told you that you should report to the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: A policeman on duty came in and told me that I had to report to the SUP building. I went there, and I was met by a policeman in a blue uniform, and I asked him why I needed to report upstairs. He told me to go up there. I went upstairs and found Vlado Sarkan [As interpreted] there. He met me, he asked me why I had come, and I told him that I was told to report to him. He told me that Kemal was doing well and that I need not to report there again, unlike other people. I went downstairs, and a former policeman, Savo - I don't know his last name - stood there. Later on he was killed by a shell. He asked me why I was there. I told him. And then he said, "Go and say hi to Kemal." I went to the corridor and I said, "Kemal, I'm here," and Kemal said to me, "Ediba go home. Don't remain here any more." He didn't know why I was there. He didn't know I was there until I said hi to him. And he simply told me that I should go home. I went home and I remained there without going out until -- unless I needed to go and get some water.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you went to -- you were told to report in the morning. Was this the morning of the day after Kemal was arrested?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you say you went upstairs and spoke with Vlado Sarkanovic, was that the second floor of the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the corridor which you spoke to Kemal -- you heard Kemal's voice, that was the first floor of the SUP building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As the witness already stated, I mean the question that was posed to the witness when she said the second floor, I mean I think that it is not in dispute any more that there is no second floor of the SUP building. There was a ground floor and first floor. So maybe just for the clarification of record, if we are talking about ground floor and first floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I guess it depends how you categorise these things. I meant -- I call it the second floor because there's a few steps, we know from the photographs taking you onto the -- as you first enter the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: If there's any confusion -- Mrs. Bobic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because -- I don't know. Maybe you can correct it. Because her answer where she met with her husband, she says it was on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I didn't meet my husband there. I simply heard his voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: -- ground floor. And Vlado Sarkanovic, it was upstairs. It wasn't the ground floor; it was the first floor, upstairs?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you later receive information that Kemal had been moved from the SUP building to the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was transferred there, but it took a long time for him to be transferred to the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say "a long time," do you mean a few days or a number of weeks?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Several weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Several weeks before you learnt that he was in the TO building; is that it?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you ever get a chance to see your husband, Kemal, during his detention in the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. My husband was beaten up in the TO building, and I heard that he was supposed to be exchanged. One young man, a policeman, told me that he would bring him to the water pump so that I could see him, because he was going to be exchanged. I prepared his underwear and a bit of money for him to come out. However, I was unable to deliver that to him because he was not exchanged on that occasion, and he remained in the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did this occur around the end of August or September of 1992, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Between August and September.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: He wasn't exchanged, but did you get a chance to see him when he was brought out to the water pump?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him. He had a very short haircut, almost no hair, and we waved to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. During your time in Bosanski Samac after the takeover and after your husband was arrested, from your house, could you hear any screams or sounds of singing coming from the SUP building and the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Certainly. It was very close, and one could hear it very well. We could hear the songs sung, and we could hear how they beat prisoners. I could recognise my husband's moans. He was beaten so badly that he was unable to get up. He was all broken up. There were worms in his wounds and I learned that from others.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, did you sometimes have the opportunity to bring food to your husband or other detainees in the TO?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were there some good guards in the TO who would bring in this food to your husband and other detainees?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Certainly. There are always some good people around.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. While your husband was detained, were you then required to perform forced labour yourself, after your husband was detained?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to forced labour up until the 25th of August, 1992, when the children swam across the Sava River. Young men crossed the Sava River, I think some 170 of them, and only us women remained, and from then on, or at least I personally, we had to go to forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said some men had swum across the river. Was this because there had been an instruction to the non-Serb men that they would have to fight with the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. That night, when the young men started fleeing, Sabahudin Nogic came, Idriz's son, and he brought a lot of papers, lists, with the names of my son; my brother-in-law; my sister's son, Nermin; and he read out their names and said they needed to report the following day to the memorial hall and that from then on they would not have a work obligation but would have to carry a Serb rifle. We sat in the corridor thinking what to do, and the young people decided immediately that they would flee across the river. While sitting in the corridor, they said to my son, "Bedrudin, don't go. If you go, your father will be killed, because your father is in the TO." So they left without anything. I didn't know where they went. And then later on, somehow we found out that they were in Croatia and that they were in the area of Orasje, around Kruza [phoen], and so on. They went bare handed. They swam across the river and left. We didn't see them until the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Bedrudin stayed with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: After your sister's son, Nermin, and others had left, was your sister, Almira, then taken to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. She and her two children, two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's Bedrija and Nermina?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, Bedrija and Nermina. Bedrija was pregnant. She had married Goran Arapovic. He swam across the river and she remained in our house. And she was taken to Zasavica just with her clothes on her back. She was in a thin summer dress.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You remained in Bosanski Samac town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And then you began to perform forced labour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Where did you have to report to be given your tasks?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: To the pensioners' hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And who would assign you then your tasks for the day at the Dom Penzionera?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: It depended on who picked us up and took us to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it men in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We had to go with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were they armed?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you have any choice about whether you went with them or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We had no choice whatsoever. We had to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you have any choice in the sort of tasks that you would perform?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you want to go to perform those tasks?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What sort of tasks were you required to do?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: I started cleaning private homes, painting them, working in them. Then I worked in the memorial hall, in the municipal building, in Pisari. I remained the longest in the PIK company. I worked there a lot. There was much to do there. I had to unload things, clean offices, load and unload, clean the bakery, silos, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say you had to unload things, what sort of things were you unloading, and from what?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: From the truck. We had to unload sacks of flour, food for chickens, and so on. God knows what they loaded on. Everything that was in the trucks and that had to be unloaded manually, we had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Who would bring in the goods in these trucks? Who were the ones who had put the -- had brought in the goods?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: People of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were they officials, people in -- either in military uniform or holding official functions in the authority, or were they just private individuals?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: The people in uniforms drove in the trucks. People who worked in offices sometimes wore uniforms and sometimes they had other, normal clothes, like they used to wear previously in offices. So there were those who wore uniforms and those who didn't at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you said that you were the ones who had to unload them. You, being you and other people who were required to do forced labour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the others that you were performing forced labour with, were they all of Muslim and Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, Croat and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone of Serb ethnicity being required to perform forced labour with you?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. They simply supervised us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were performing your forced labour, did you wear the white armbands that you told the Chamber about?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, we wore them; and later on, we took them off, without asking anybody. And they didn't warn us about it later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were working in the PIK factory or in other locations, did you ever see any of the defendants? Did you ever see Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: He came to see Stevan Tutnjevic, upstairs, in the offices that I had cleaned and painted, together with other people that worked with me there. So I painted them. I just put everything in proper order, put up curtains, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And this is in the PIK factory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. I saw him in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Miroslav Tadic, did you ever see him while you were performing your forced labour?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Sometimes he would come, but he wouldn't greet us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say he would come, do you mean he would come to the PIK factory?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were performing this forced labour, did you ever receive payment?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We did not receive compensation and money. Sometimes they would give us some flour and some bread.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Who would give you the flour and the bread?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. They used to work on the ground floor. Let me just recollect. Borojevic. Borojevic issued us a paper stating that we were allowed to get flour for bread. He used for work in the PIK factory. I think his first name was Boro, Boro Borojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And did this happen on a regular basis --

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No, only sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: During the whole time that you performed forced labour, would you say this happened once or more than once? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: I worked in the PIK factory for several months. We received flour a couple of times in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have to work every day once you started your forced labour assignment?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And whilst you were performing your forced labour, were you supervised by armed personnel?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. Let me tell you: Once we entered through the gate, there was a receptionist, a guard there, who was armed, but inside they didn't guard us with uniforms. We had our tasks. We had to clean and do other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And would you ever be accompanied by armed persons if you were being taken to certain locations to perform tasks? So, for example, when you went to Pisari, you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. That man always had a rifle. He was not a nice man. He was -- he had bad manners and he did not have education, any education.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And this man would accompany you, whilst armed, when you were being taken to locations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was constantly drunk and he was causing all kinds of incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions just about your own property and shops and that that you ran in Bosanski Samac. Was the property from your shops, first, from the establishments you ran, was that looted or stolen during the period of time that you were in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let us begin with the Sedrvan. Sedrvan was a little bit away from our house. It was a catering facility. Some things were taken away and the window panes were broken. There was glass everywhere. My husband was in Batkovici, and there was a man by the name of Cviko Stevanovic. I didn't know him. He came to my door and he said that we had to hand our property over to him before being exchanged. This man by the name of Cvijetin --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you questions about this man later and his seizing of your property. I was just wondering if before he came to take away property, were other items belonging to you looted, anything from your shops, your vehicles? Were your vehicles taken from you?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the vehicles were requisitioned. Cera and Laki came for the vehicles. When Kemal was taken to the camp, to the police station, a day later, three lads came. I didn't know one of them, but I also didn't know yet another one of them who had no fingers, but later on I learned that his name was Laki. Cera was with him, and this man Laki asked for the papers for the Renault car. He said that we had to give them everything, and he even put a rifle into my son's mouth, saying that we had to give them all the papers. They took the papers and took the car away. Then Petar came and took the Skoda. As for the other two cars, first they took off the licence plates and then they also took the vehicles. It's really hard for me to remember everything, because you can't take notes or anything. These are really hard times.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I understand that, Mrs. Bobic. So if I've understood you correctly, you had four vehicles. Two of them were taken -- they came to your house and demanded papers and keys, and the others were simply stolen some night?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You mentioned that your husband was transferred to Batkovici from the TO building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the winter of 1992, that's when all the cars -- I'm sorry. That's when all the people were taken from the SUP building to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how did you learn that your husband had been taken to Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I only learnt about that when I got his message, but we saw the bus when it arrived. It was standing there in front of the SUP building and the TO building. We didn't know why. But they took all the people out of the buildings, tied their eyes with white cloth, and took them in an unknown direction. We didn't know where they were until we started receiving the first messages from the Red Cross, the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you witnessed the men being taken away, but at that time you didn't know where; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And later you received information through the International Red Cross that they were in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you on one occasion have an opportunity to visit your husband in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did the man you've mentioned, Cvijetin Stevanovic bring you to see your husband?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was this man Cvetijn Stevanovic from Bosanski Samac or was he from a neighbouring area?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: That man was not from Bosanski Samac. He was from Obudovac, Pelagicevo. At that time, I didn't know where he was from until my husband returned from the camp, I didn't know where he was headquartered.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And this man, Cvetijn Stevanovic, he came and brought you to visit your husband in Batkovici. Did he tell you why you were going to see your husband?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. At first I didn't know why we were going there. Let me tell you: He married my sister's daughter by force. She had been married to a person in Brcko before that. But when people were gathered up in Brcko, people were taken to Loncari, and then he forced my niece to marry him, and he heard from her about our property. He then went to Batkovici and then came to us one day. He took all the papers pertaining to our property from SUP, both mine and my sister's, because we shared the same household. We two sisters were married to two brothers. He picked up those papers and again came to pick me up, telling me that I had to go with him to Batkovici. He then went to Batkovici and asked Kemal to sign this piece of paper, indicating that all the property would be transferred to him, that this all belonged to him now. My son and myself had to load things onto his car. Then they came with the cars and they took three or four days to pick everything up. They took whatever took their fancy, and it turned out that he would be living in our house. Kemal signed this piece of paper for him and he was released. He came to Samac and said that all the property no longer belonged to us; it belonged to him now. And he started taking all the things that were light enough for him to carry into his car. Later on, he came with the trucks from the 4th [As interpreted], at least that's what I heard, from the people who were gathering the stuff. I heard that the Banja Luka Corps, that was stationed in his house, that they came to pick all those things up. They took everything out, and it was snowing outside. It lasted three or four days. That's how long it took them to carry all the things away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Bobic. I think this is just a question of clarification for the transcript. You said: "Later on he came with the trucks from the 4th," and did you say anything after "4th"? "Trucks from the 4th." We don't have anything after "4th."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. That was the 4th Corps, the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, these events happened at the end of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. This happened in 1993, when I was supposed to be exchanged with my family. My husband was exchanged in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Mrs. Bobic. Sorry. I meant the end of 1993. So after this man had succeeded in forcing your husband to sign over his property while he was detained, were you able to stay on in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I remained there until the exchange, and I was exchanged on the 24th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions now for -- did you stay in your own house after this man had taken away the property you described?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We stayed in our house, but we only used the business premises that were downstairs and the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Bobic, after your property had been taken from you, did you take a decision that you wanted to try to leave Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I had made that decision even earlier, but there was no opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And why had you taken that decision to try to leave Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: All the Muslims and Croats who lived in Bosanski Samac, we had a really hard life. Every night we expected something bad to happen. We didn't have a real life because I couldn't make the decision to leave Bosanski Samac, because all my property was there, but I had to do it because of the hard life that we had. My son was seriously ill and he had to go every day out for the work obligation. And when he came back home, I didn't have any medicines to give him or any way to help him.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you had decided that you had to leave Bosanski Samac, who did you go to see about trying to leave Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me tell you: I had to seek out Mr. Miro, Brko, Tadic. All the small fry that I talked to were no good. I had to talk -- had to find him, because he was the main man in charge of all this. He had to write our names down in the book of people to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I just ask the usher if I could see photograph 46 from Exhibit P14.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, let me ask you one question while we get the photograph. Where did you go see Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I went in front of the municipal building, because this is how you got in touch with all the important people who still held their functions. It was very difficult for me to get into the municipal building. Mr. Antic wouldn't let me. He was an armless man - he didn't have an arm - and he stood there at the reception desk. He told me that I couldn't go in without a new ID card. I only had an old, Yugoslav ID card. But I did stay there, and I had the opportunity to go upstairs in the municipal building. A man whom I didn't know well helped me. So I went upstairs. The first contact about my exchange was with Mr. -- with Dr. Blagoje Simic, who received me in his office. He treated me really nice. There was first a young girl who received me and then I went into his office. He asked me, "Why, ma'am, are you leaving Bosanski Samac? This will pass. Everything will be fine." I told him, "No. I have to go. I keep trying to treat my son. He has no strength left to walk at all." And then he told me that I had to go to see Miro Brko. That's where we ended our conversation. He told me that Miro Brko's office was to the right of his office. So I got in. I talked to him. He told me that I had to tell him how many people wanted to be exchanged and I had to give him 12.000 German marks for all of us and my husband to be exchanged. So we made a deal, we spoke a longer period of time, and then he remained in his office, I went back home. We met the next day and I gave him the amount in an envelope.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I just ask you to have a look at the photograph that is on the ELMO beside you? Mrs. Bobic, is this the building in which you say that the meetings and discussions about your exchange took place?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And in this building you met both Mr. Blagoje Simic and Mr. Miroslav Tadic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm finished with the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You've told us that Miroslav Tadic told you he had to give you [sic] 12.000 Deutschmarks in order to be exchanged. Did he explain to you why you had to pay him money?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, for us to be able to leave. He didn't say much. He said, "If you want to leave, you have to have money. If you don't have money, you cannot go."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Reidy. Just for the sake of the record. Line 15, page 44, you actually said in your question: "You've told us that Miroslav Tadic told you he had to give you 12.000 Deutschmarks." Maybe we should just sort of amend the record to identify what perhaps you meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I intended to say:

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You told us that Miroslav Tadic told you that you had to give him money in order to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, you said that you came back the next day and you gave him the amount he requested. Was that also to the municipal building that you pointed out in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it in the office or was it in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: In the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic give you a receipt for the money you gave him?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did he tell you any information right there and then when you could expect to be exchanged or what would happen next?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: We heard that there would be an exchange, and since we weren't on the list, it wasn't really simple for us to put our names on the list. Our children were asking for us in Orasje, and I also -- also my family in Zasavica were sick and tired of everything. I'm talking about my sister's children. I had to keep in touch with him for us to be exchanged, because that was the last chance for us to go out. So we were all sitting around talking about how we could leave. I spoke to him. I asked him about my husband, Kemal, whether he would also be exchanged. He said, "No problem." He would be there. A car from the fire department would go and pick him up. But the day of the exchange came, the 24th of December. We went out to be exchanged. I looked around and saw that Kemal was not there. We came to Dragalic. He was not there. Kemal was not there either.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
