utterances.text: Thank you. You gave Miroslav Tadic the money. Approximately how many days after you gave him the money did you find out that you would be put on the exchange list?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of December I gave him the money, and then one, two, or three days later I learned that we were under number 50, Ediba Bobic and my son Bedrudin, and then number 51 was Almira Bobic, and number 52 was Bedrija Arapovic and the little child that was born there, or maybe it was Bedrija Bobic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters are not sure.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: And the little baby who was born in Zasavica camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On the 12th of December, 1993, [Indiscernible] who came round with the list where you saw your name, as you've said, under 50, and that of your relatives under 51 and 52?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said she gave the money on the 12th of December, but she didn't say that she saw the list on that day but that it was in fact later. And then the question is trying to -- through the question, it is trying to -- the Prosecution is trying to indicate that it was on that very same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I didn't try to do that at all. I just wanted to make clear that we were talking about December 1993. The witness had said earlier -- and the witness did say this was one to three days afterwards that she learnt about her relatives. So I apologise if it came across that I was trying change that record. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: But Mrs. Bobic, my question is: Who brought round the list with -- where you saw your name and that of your relatives on?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: The courier. I don't know what to call that person. The receptionist. That was the person that informed people about the fact that they were on the list for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was Kemal's name alongside yours and Bedrudin's?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't on that piece of paper, because we were leaving from Samac, and Kemal was supposed to come from Batkovici, because that's where he was at that time. He was not in Bosanski Samac, but we were hoping that we would meet at Dragalic together.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And one thing for the record. The interpreters didn't catch the full name of one of your relatives. Is it Bedrija Arapovic Bobic? Is that the full name of your niece?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. The full name is Bedrija Bobic, Arapovic being her married name. She gave birth to a daughter in Zasavica. Her husband swam across the Sava River and she remained in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. How many days after you saw your name on the list did the exchange actually occur?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Five or six days later, because we went to be exchanged on the 24th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you given instructions about what you could take with you?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Just our personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And where were you told that you should go on the 24th of December?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: At 7.00 a.m. we were supposed to report to the pensioners' home. The bus was supposed to come and pick us up there and drive us to be exchanged in Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Bobic. When you say that you could just take your personal belongings with you, what does that mean? Does it mean one bag, two bags? What exactly does "personal belongings" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the clothes that could fit into a bag, all the things that we could fit into a bag. We couldn't take much more. You know what kinds of items are considered personal belongings: Clothes, some cosmetics, and I also took pictures of my son's funeral. The funeral had been -- photographs had been taken of it. I didn't have the opportunity to look at it. And I took it with me. And Mirko [As interpreted] checked our luggage, and when he came to the photographs, asked me -- he asked me very angrily [As interpreted], "Why are you taking this," and I told him, "Miro, if something like this had happened to you, you would be taking photographs with you too."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. But just one clarification, Ms. Reidy. Line 18, it says "Mirko checked our luggage." Can we clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The person who checked your bags --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another objection to the interpretation. The witness said, "I responded angrily," and here on page 48, line 20, it says that he was angry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both he and I were angry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the person who checked your bag, could you just repeat his name for us?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Miro Brko checked our bags.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you had one bag with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Miro Brko, Mr. Tadic, did he check your bags when you assembled at the Dom Penzionera?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had to get into a room one by one, and he went through our bags.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did he explain to you why he was searching your bags?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did he check the bags of Bedrudin as well?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of all of us who were there to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And amongst you all who were there, what was the ethnicity? Were you all Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You testified there were a number of buses that came to the Dom Penzionera. Were there already some people on the buses when you boarded them?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: They had come from Zasavica. The other bus came from Zasavica before, or in fact when we boarded the bus, the bus came from Zasavica. There were the people who had been imprisoned there and also the Croats who were to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say "also the Croats who were to be exchanged," are these Croats from villages in Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were these people who were taken from their villages or people who had been detained in a detention unit?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: The people who came on the bus were the people who were -- who had been in Zasavica, who lived in Zasavica, and those who were detained in Zasavica. And we were the people who lived either in our own homes or in somebody else's houses, but we had a separate bus. We boarded it in front of the pensioners' home building. We didn't have any contact with the other bus, because we didn't board that bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, the bus drove you, you said, eventually to Dragalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Dragalic is on the -- well, in Croatia, on the border, is it?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you arrived at Dragalic, were there other people who were there who you were to be exchanged for?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We hoped there would be an exchange. However, nobody boarded the buses that went back to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So when you arrived at Dragalic, was there anybody there from the other side to meet you or ...

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. We had to keep on waiting. We had to wait for an entry visa to enter Croatia, because we didn't have papers to disembark in Croatia. We had to wait there for a long time. There were thunder showers that night. It wasn't very pleasant. It wasn't an exchange where people were exchanged one by one. That wasn't that type of exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm going to come back and ask you about that, but just let me ask you: When you arrived at Dragalic, was Miroslav Tadic also with you?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was among the people escorting.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, you said that it wasn't an exchange where people were exchanged one by one. What happened to you? Were you exchanged for anybody at all or were you just simply transferred across to Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We were expelled and sent to Croatian territory. It was very difficult for us in Croatia, until we came to Orasje, because we were unable to remain in Croatia until we got papers from the Orasje government, stating that we would be allowed to go to Domaljevac or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you arrived at night at Dragalic. Were you required to dismount from the buses and then cross across to Croatian-held territory? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We crossed, but it was in a bus, to the Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you see representatives of the International Red Cross there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you asked, when you crossed over, whether or not you were leaving Bosanski Samac of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked us anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did Miroslav Tadic ask you that when he was checking your bags back in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: He didn't ask us anything. He was probably glad to expel us from there as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you arrived at Dragalic, did you in fact see Kemal there?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. Kemal remained in Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When was Kemal finally exchanged?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Kemal was exchanged on the 6th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I said I finished my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Cross-examination. Who is going to start? Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just have ten seconds to confer with my client, to check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please. (Mr. Vukovic, not Krgovic)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vukovic. You will start. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Srdjan Vukovic. I am an attorney and I will be asking you a few questions on behalf of Dr. Blagoje Simic regarding your testimony today, as well as your statements given to the Prosecution in 1995 and in 2001. You said today that a policeman came and took all of you to the house of Idriz Nogic.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That happened some two days after the armed conflict. Can we agree that that policeman in fact took you to some kind of a shelter?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: We can agree regarding that, but I have to add that he rounded us all up, and it is possible that we would fare worse if we remained in our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So we can say that he took you there for your own personal safety and security?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible, or at least they also could have wanted to see how many of us there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, in your statement given in 2002, in paragraph 22, you stated as follows: "Two days after they searched our house for weapons, a Serb policeman came and told us we could not stay and that we should go to a shelter." After that, in paragraph 23 of that same statement, you said as follows: "Almost all people who lived between the Spomen Dom and our house were in that shelter, although some were finding shelter elsewhere." So we can agree, can't we, that Serb policemen took you, for your own safety, to the house of Idriz Nogic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I think that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is now -- I've let it go one question, but this is purely speculation as to the purpose of what the police were doing. The witness was asked in chief: "Were you told why you were being moved?" And the witness said: "No. We were given no information as to why we should move out of our home." So counsel can make arguments he wants, but now he's speculating, I think having the witness testified that they were given a reason what the reason -- the motivation of the police, and that is purely speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't see it that way, because counsel has been referring to the statements made by the witness, and it's from those statements that he's able to ask the question the way he has put it, that could this be the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Well, absolutely, Your Honour. I was hoping that's exactly what would happen, because that's why when he quoted from a statement, I would see -- thought he might get there, but he didn't. His question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Anyway, Ms. Reidy, I don't see anything wrong with the cross-examination. The counsel will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would just like to clarify this. I quoted what the witness stated in paragraph 22, in her statement given to the Prosecution in May of 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just go ahead with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Bobic, in the same statement, in the same paragraph, you went on to say that on that night, when you were taken to Idriz Nogic's house, there was shelling. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Where were the shells coming from? Where was the town shelled from?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. We were in the basement. We just heard that tanks were rumbling down our street, and we couldn't see anything from the basement, because one just couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you perhaps learn of this on another day, on the following day, during the time you remained in Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I didn't learn anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how frequent was the shelling of Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: It lasted a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately? Was it once a week? Twice a week? During what period of time? Was it in 1992 or in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Both in 1992 and in 1993, and then I was exchanged, and then 1994 and 1995 is when I travelled further on. But all the way up until that time, there was shelling going on, but I was so scared that I couldn't really try to retain the information on when that happened. I lost all count of time after February 14th, and now I live because I have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: But we can agree that the town of Samac was constantly shelled?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't constantly shelled, but we lived in great fear. We weren't only afraid of shells. We were also afraid of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you something else. You stated that your son, Bedrudin, had work obligation and that he had, among other things, to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And then today you said that he would tell you every evening where he spent his day, performing which tasks?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber: Where did your son dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: He dug trenches in the direction of Grebnice, because Grebnice were called death graves or graveyards [As interpreted], because we knew how dangerous that situation was. We knew that they took our children to go and dig those trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: All I wanted to learn was where did he go to dig trenches. In addition to Grebnice, did he go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No, because after he became sick, he was transferred to lighter tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: Why were the trenches dug around Grebnice?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Serb soldiers would be able to answer that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did your son, by any chance, tell you whether there was an exchange of fire while he was digging trenches as part of his work obligation?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: The first fire that was opened and that he witnessed was by Mile Pancir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, no. I'm interested in the lines of separation. Was there any fire exchange there?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the Prosecution in 1995, you stated that one of the shells fell on your house.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It fell on the summer kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And when was that? What month was it? What year?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: It was in 1992. But as to the rest, I can't tell you which month it was. I don't know whether Kemal was already arrested then or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Bobic, in your statement, you said that when you went to the SUP building, you were greeted by Savo, who was killed later on.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Was Savo killed by a shell?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I can't give you any dates, but let me tell you this: He was a wonderful man.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, can you just give us the year?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: 1992. He was killed by the well, where there used to be a mosque, near the main road, by the department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So we will agree that it's basically the centre of Bosanski Samac, downtown?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was in Pere Bosica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the Prosecutor in 2002, you stated that some men who were in the house of Idriz Nogic had to carry sandbags as part of their work obligation.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that these sandbags are used to protect the buildings and windows from shelling?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Bobic, you said that as part of your work obligation you went plum-picking?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber where you went, to which location.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: It was somewhere in Odzak municipality. I couldn't tell you which field it was and who was the owner. We simply went there to pick plums and load them. We were then escorted by a young man, Despic. We had to pick plums all day long, from morning until night.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear, by any chance, whether there was any shelling there?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement given to the Prosecution, you said that you saw Mr. Blagoje Simic in the municipal building when you went to ask that your husband be released from prison?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us: When was that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: It was on the 11th of December of 1993. ^can you tell us: In which office did you see Mr. Simic in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which office did you see Mr. Simic in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I saw him in the office where municipal presidency was, on the right-hand side, last door. There was a very nice young lady there who allowed me to go and see this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the only time when you saw Mr. Simic in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. This is why I went to the municipal building. I asked to go to be exchanged, then I went to see him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: How was Mr. Simic dressed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: He did not wear a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: How did he look? Did he have a beard?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't have a beard, and he was just as always, very approachable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, you gave a statement to the Prosecution on the 14th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In that statement, you never mentioned seeing Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I contacted Mr. Simic in his office. I don't know whether there was a mistake in translation. I can't tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, all I'm saying is that in your statement given to the Prosecution in 1995, you never mentioned seeing Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I did see Mr. Simic, and Mr. Simic must remember me, because he knows me well. My husband played chess with his family. We were not very close friends, but we knew each other well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, is it possible that we are talking about Mr. Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. Milan Simic was in a wheelchair at that time. He was in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me, please: Who did your husband play chess with?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: With Milan's father, Vojin Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. I have to ask you something else, and please don't take me wrong. In your statement given to the Prosecution, both in 1995 and in 2002, you stated that your son was a member of the organisation called MOS, M-O-S, which stands for Muslim Youth Party?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what is MOS.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I think that MOS was there to associate young people in a religious way, so that young people would know who they were religiouswise, so they would know that they were of Muslim faith. Because at that time, young people didn't know what faith they had. They were really not going to mosques and so on, so this organisation served to associate them religiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put you another short question regarding that. Was MOS the wing of the SDA, the youth wing of that party?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: After the shelling of Samac, which took place two days after the 17th, was there electricity and water in town?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. For a while we had both electricity and water, and then later on it was cut off and we didn't have any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And can we agree that that lasted for quite a while?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that all residents of Samac were without electricity and water?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that there were food shortages as well?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Everybody had humanitarian aid except for us Muslims. It didn't come our way because we were not called when the humanitarian aid was distributed. We knew that it had arrived, because our people were unloading it, but nobody called us when they were distributing that food.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You stated here before this Trial Chamber, and also in your statements, that your property was seized?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And you clarified in which manner?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, but also our cafe or shop was destroyed, and you didn't ask me about that. It was destroyed after I was exchanged, some year or two after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you: What is the status of your property now?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: The shop was destroyed. The property was literally returned to us but is in such a condition that we could not move in. One would have to invest a lot of money in order to be able to move in, because there's no bathroom or anything else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mrs. Bobic, we will agree that you stated yourself that a shell had fallen on your house?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No . I said that there was one shell that landed on the summer kitchen, but my house was so strong that a cannon would be unable to destroy it. It was a brick house, a three-storey house, so nothing could destroy that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, you just told us that the property had been returned to you, legally?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So the real estate that was in your name was returned?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: The house was returned, and some other things are to be returned yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: But all of this is under way, the process is under way?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we ask for a break, Your Honours, ten-minute break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Why do you want a break? We shall have a break at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Your Honours, but we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The next counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Madam Ediba.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: My name is Borislav Pisarevic. I'm an attorney from Samac, and I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Simo Zaric. Before I ask any questions, I would like to extend to you, on behalf of Mr. Simo Zaric, his sincere regret for everything that your family and yourself have been through in those retched events in the former Yugoslavia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in our own town of Samac. I'm going to ask you just a couple of questions. I would kindly ask you to try and answer the questions with yes or no, or if you don't know the answer, please say so. If you have failed to understand the question, please say so and I will repeat it. My questions will mainly pertain to the period up until the 17th of April, 1992, that is, up until the time when the conflict broke out in the town of Bosanski Samac. I would like to make sure that you understood me quite well as to the topic of our conversation. Did you understand me properly?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did I understand, but I can answer all of your questions, but only about the events up until the 14th of February, because after that period -- after that date, I have to tell you that I wouldn't be able to tell you anything, because that was after the death of my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you've already stated in the course of your testimony that you do know about the existence of the 4th Detachment, can you confirm the fact that the establishment of the 4th Detachment was a public affair, that the 4th Detachment -- the establishment of the 4th Detachment was broadcast over the radio and also in the media? How do you know about the existence of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear it over the radio, but I worked in an area where one could learn a lot. You, Boro, you know it yourself, and so does my neighbour, Mr. Simo Zaric. You were making the 4th Detachment composed of the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly. I'll be asking you questions about that later. So it was no secret that the 4th Detachment was established in Bosanski Samac, I mean the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was not a part of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that the 4th Detachment was not part of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. It was part of it, but in Bosanski Samac there were no people from Yugoslavia in the 4th Detachment. They were only people from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll take a break for 20 minutes and resume at 12.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. Cross-examination continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, are you aware of the fact that in the 4th Detachment there were representatives of all the ethnic communities, I mean Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and other ethnic communities that lived in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: In the 4th Detachment there were, first of all, the Yugoslav People's Army that had come with their vehicles, and the people who had been transported to Bosanski Samac, because they walked around the town, they were in those units. I'm sure that Mr. Simo Zaric had brought them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, ma'am. I have to interrupt you. We're talking about the period up to the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, up until the 17th of April, because they were moving around even before that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: My question to you was: Who were the members of the 4th Detachment, and what were their ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, it was well known. They were Muslims and Serbs. I don't know whether there were any Croats or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You now mentioned the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you whether you know that in the municipalities of Samac, Pelagicevo, Brcko, Gradacac, there was the 17th Tactical Group of the Yugoslav People's Army that had been established.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, please don't ask me that, because I don't know about that. But I do know who was walking around Samac, and I do know who was inducted into the 4th Corps by Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So to conclude: You do not know that the 17th Tactical Group of the Yugoslav People's Army was formed in Samac, Pelagicevo, Brcko, Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I do know that there were troops around, and they entered Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Radovan Antic was?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Radovan Antic was a teacher in the school, and he worked in the staff, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Radovan Antic was the commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I don't know. I would like to apologise. I don't think I could talk about this topic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Mr. Zaric, together with Vlado Sarkanovic; Milos Simandic [phoen]; Djordje Pisarevic, nicknamed Ruka; and Mihalj Topolovac; on the night when your son tragically died, that he came and expressed his sympathies to you and your family?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm the fact that at your son's funeral there was a large number of inhabitants of the town of Samac of Serb, Muslim, and other ethnicities, that lived in Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: I didn't attend my son's funeral, but I did notice a lot of things from the photographs. But Simo Zaric was my neighbour. He was not on any of the pictures anywhere near.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly. Do you know that a citizens' rally was held in the cinema hall in Samac following this event when this tragic event was discussed and the events in Bosanski Samac as a whole?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you that, because I know only about the things that happened until the 14th of February. Everybody knows that I was in my home after that and that doctors came to give me shots every day in the morning and in the afternoon, so I wouldn't really know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned that you had your work obligation in the PIK factory, that's the agri business complex.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us and confirm the fact that the manager of that company was Stevan Tutnjevic, nicknamed Stona [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm the fact that you worked there in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm the fact that at that time you saw Mr. Zaric on one occasion going to see the manager, Stevan Tutnjevic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Bobic. My name is Novak Lukic. I'm an attorney, and I'm the Defence counsel for Mr. Miroslav Tadic. I will be conducting my cross-examination on his behalf. I believe that I will take some more time than my colleagues. I will first be asking you about some general facts and then some more specific questions pertaining to my client, and I would also like to ask you some questions relating to your credibility as a witness. I will also, like my colleagues, ask you to answer my questions very briefly. If you want to clarify a point pertaining to my questions, we can leave that to the Prosecutor, who can then ask the questions in re-direct. I keep being cautioned by the Trial Chamber and by the interpreters that I speak too fast, and in order to avoid the overlapping of my questions and your answers, I would kindly ask you to make a pause before answering, because my question has to be interpreted for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, and if you start speaking too fast, then it is not -- everything is not interpreted. I want to clarify one thing: You talked to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor twice, as far as I know. Do you remember that you spoke to the representatives of the Prosecution for the first time in February 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 14th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It obviously is a very important date in your life?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, a very difficult one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first interview that you had with the Prosecution was on the anniversary of your son's death?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you were given the statement that you gave to the Prosecution for signature. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second time that you spoke to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor was on the 18th and the 20th of May this year. My learned colleague Ms. Reidy spoke to you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not sign that statement, but as far as I understand, when you arrived here in The Hague, you went through the statement in detail with the Prosecution and you stand by what you said there?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to ask you any questions about the death of your son. We did discuss this at length before this Trial Chamber. From what I could see, his girlfriend was a Serb. This is what it says in the statement?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was her name?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Gordana Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does she still live in Samac? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have to tell you: They were dating. They were supposed to get married, because Gordana Arapovic and Bedrija got married after this event. They had to get married -- I still don't know what happened that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I really don't want to go into that. Do you know that the accused Miroslav Tadic had a son whose name is also Miroslav Tadic and that he was on friendly terms -- he was a good friend of both your sons?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a nice lad. He was friendly both with me and my husband and my sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he was friends with your son because they were of the same generation?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were of the same generation, but they were good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, to clarify some events a bit more, I would like to ask that the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour. I have a copy of the map that we already used, that's D27/3, and I would like that to be placed in front of the witness for her to mark -- to make some markings there. I'm interested in three buildings: The house of the witness; the Nogics' house, where they took shelter; and where their cafe was. This is a clean copy, without any markings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not really very good with maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, if you can find your way around this map, then please do show me, but if not, we will not be dwelling upon this. So could you please explain to the Trial Chamber where your house was.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. I don't know whether this is the main street, or is this the street running parallel to the Sava River? Could you please assist me with that? I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we will not, then, do anything with this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not be insisting on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your husband will be testifying next, and I believe that he will be able to do so, to assist us. At any rate, my question to you is the following: You said that you lived in Ivo Lola Ribar Street?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this street in the immediate vicinity of the Sava River, or in other words, is it the second street parallel to the main street, which is parallel to -- which is located where the SUP and TO are?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where was your hamburger stand?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: From the crossroads, from the Spomen Dom or the memorial hall, it was to the left or the front of the school where children played football. At the entrance -- across the road from the entrance to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we could say that it was in front of the elementary school and the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, in that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the Trial Chamber is quite familiar with where these two buildings are. You already answered questions asked by my colleague Mr. Vukovic regarding your accommodation in the house belonging to Mr. Nogic. Do you know that in the immediate vicinity of that house, there was the house of the goldsmith, Paroli [phoen], where people were also housed, as in a shelter?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: It was in another street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the shelters were marked with arrows pointing to them at that time in Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, the building where we were was not marked, because it was not a proper shelter; it was just a basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you stated today that you returned to your home of your own free will and that you took shelter below the stairs when the shelling was going on?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 12/12 of the transcript, I will now move on to another topic, the events after the 17th of April - so today you stated - that's line 12, page 12 - you said: "During the first days, we felt that we could not go out." I wanted to ask you about this term "felt." Did somebody order you not to go out or did you yourself decide not to go out?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No, we did not decide, but the moment when the first shell fell in front of the SUP building, we no longer went out. We weren't moving around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way I understood it. You also described -- we heard your description of the events in the night between the 16th and the 17th of April. Do you remember whether your husband went out into the yard or into the street that night?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: My house has two entrances, the entrance and the exit from the yard. I went into the yard because I heard some people walking there, but I didn't hear any voices. So I opened the door and turned on the light, and one of them said, "I'll shoot. Turn off the light." I don't know who it was, because there was a lot of panic at that time. When a shot was fired, there was a very strong explosion, in fact. So I don't know whether he went to the other side, because our -- the corridor in our house was 18 metres long. We couldn't see each other in the dark. So I don't know whether he went out on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony, responding to questions asked by the Prosecution, that Savo, the police officer, told you that Kemal was detained there in the SUP. Is that correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this Savo Savic, the man who was a police officer even before the war?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was after your husband was detained?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, I have information that Savo Savic was killed on the 17th of April, 1992. Do you have that information too? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date of his death. I do know that he helped me to get in touch with Kemal. That's when Kemal told me to go home. I think it was him. It wasn't anyone else. I remember his face quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I will ask you a few questions. We also heard about the distribution of the humanitarian aid. You said that in the first few days you did receive some humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Did you consider yourself to be quite well off in relation to other families in Samac, taking into account the kind of income that you had at your disposal, or were you among the poorer families?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I never made any difference as to who I socialised with, which people they belonged to, but at that time, when they distributed milk, we all got out. And I don't know why we couldn't get any food later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that later on, when major shortages of food started occurring, that humanitarian aid was distributed only to those citizens who did not have any income or who had very low income?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell me: It was the fact that many people got things from various places. I was excluded from these groups. I don't know why it was, whether we were members of the SDA or whether we had more property. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your neighbours, Muslims and Croats, did receive humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: It's possible that they received it on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you the date, whether it was in 1992 or 1993, but I do know that on one occasion the humanitarian aid came and they said that somebody from an Islamic community sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have document D44/3 shown to the witness. [In English] Put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will put it on the ELMO so you can look at it both on your screen or you can look at it directly. Mrs. Bobic, do you see the date here in the top part of this document? Please have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: 1992. I know that this didn't happen then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in May 1992, that the town of Samac was divided into quarters or neighbourhoods and that this is how the food was distributed?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: It didn't come to our quarter or neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please check whether there are any Muslims and Croats on this list. Do you maybe know anyone?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown document D45/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document, Mrs. Bobic. It is dated 18th of August, 1992, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We didn't experience this. We did not receive any aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know any of the people on this list? They are your fellow citizens. There are Muslims and Croats here.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, there are names here of people that I know, but I don't know whether they received any aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any of these people live in your vicinity?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, Dzakic Mujo lived nearby, but I don't know whether he received aid. These are people that resided in Samac, but I don't know whether they ever received any aid. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the warehouse of the Red Cross in Bosanski Samac municipality was located in the house of Irfan Jakupovic, which is near your house? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. I know that there was a warehouse in the old hotel. This is where we loaded and unloaded the goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the warehouse of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Red Cross. In 1992 there was no Red Cross in my street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you knew Irfo Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did. He's the father of Dario.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he's a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he perished too?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you, Mrs. Bobic, know that somebody who dug trenches in Grebnice was killed while digging them in Grebnice?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I can't go back to those years. It's very difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you spent almost two years in Samac after the war broke out, do you know that over 400 people, somebody's sons were killed in combat near Samac?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that. Sons of some of the people that I socialised with were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today you described to us how you saw your husband when he went to the well, artesian well, and you described what condition he was in.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your 1995 statement, on page 3 of the B/C/S version, which is -- let me just assist my learned friends from the Prosecution -- page 00258169 of the English version, you said as follows: "Once I saw my husband at the time when he was detained at the TO. It happened when I visited Fatima, who lived in an apartment next to the TO. From her balcony, I could see down into the yard of the TO. I saw my husband in the yard of the TO. I could see that he was completely bruised. I could see his haircut was cut short. We waved to each other." Do you remember stating this in 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did it happen exactly as you described it?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you saw him and you waved to each other?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: When I was on Fatima's balcony, they were all walking in a circle. I waved to him. Now, whether he recognised me or not, I don't know. We just waved to each other. Everybody raised their hands when they saw us there. It was close. It was on the third floor, and he was in the TO yard. So we weren't that close, and we couldn't see each other that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, did you see your husband?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised his body build, because he's a very large man to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you talked to the Prosecutor this year, you said, in paragraph 42, regarding that same event, as follows: "I saw a large number of prisoners walking in a circle. They had shaven heads. I couldn't see whether Kemal was among them. I cried and my hat fell off. That was before I saw Kemal at the artesian well."

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but that is completely wrong statement. First of all, I didn't have high blood -- high sugar blood level. I saw him from Fatima's balcony because they were all walking in a circle. They were with short hair, some of them had beards, some didn't. Everybody waved and he waved too. I saw that it was somebody that looked like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This statement was read out to you this year --

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm telling you everything that I saw from Fatima's balcony. I'm not lying at all. I don't like lying. I'm telling the truth. And everything that I experienced I'm telling you about now. I went to Fatima's apartment and I stood there waiting for the people to come out for a walk. I looked there. All of them were circling, walking in a circle. I waved. All of them waved back. They looked at me. And among them I recognised my husband, who was in the TO, walking with them in a circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what is stated in this statement given in May of 2002 is not correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you that. I didn't quite understand your question. I'm telling you how it was. I'm giving you my account of what I had experienced. I'm not trying at all to cheat you or the other side. I'm telling you about what I had experienced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm making an intervention for the sake of the record, because there's -- I thought this might be clarified, but this is a strange phrase, which I don't think Mr. Lukic meant to say. First line of page 78. In the English, it reads: "I cried and my head fell off." I don't know if that's what Mr. Lukic read out, but my -- the statement is that, you know, I was crying and my sugar blood level was low." And the witness has again talked about her blood levels. I think she knows what she was talking about. It may be in the translation, the phrase "my head fell off" came across instead of something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we don't dwell on this topic, but in B/C/S version, in paragraph 42, it says: "I cried. My sugar blood level was low," and in the English it says the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: It says "my head fell off."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Anyway, it's been corrected. Can you move on, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right, Mrs. Bobic. We will now turn to another topic. And I'm interested now in something that can be found in your statement given on the 18th and 22nd of May, 2002, which we did not touch upon today, and that pertains to your trip to Zasavica, paragraph 45. You described in detail how the trucks came, how your niece, who was pregnant, at the time, was put in a truck and you went on to say as follows: "They came in a truck to the house and forced all of us to go. My niece was in a dress and the others were rounded up in the street. I got off the truck. I didn't want to leave the house and I wanted to wait for my son to come back from forced labour." Do you remember stating that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that's what I would like to clarify. You got on the truck and then you decided to get off?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I decided on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And nobody prevented you from doing that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, there was nobody there. These people went into another yard, so I got off the truck with my things, and I came into the house in order to wait for my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that was in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from that August of 1992 until December of 1993, nobody force forced you to go to Zasavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Nobody came looking for me. I remained there. I went to perform my work obligation, and I can't tell you how I managed to get out of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Mrs. Bobic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: If you're not going to take very long. If it's going to be very long, then I would like to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. How much time do you need? If you can reorganise. You know that the witness is quite stressed, so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to cover the exchanges and so on. But before that I would like to ask the witness a few questions regarding her credibility, because that's quite an interesting topic for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, I read for the first time, in your May 2002 statement, in paragraph 83, how you described your attempts to have your property returned to you, and you said that you went to Pelagicevo a few times to see how you could get your property returned: "When I went on the fourth occasion, I was told that I couldn't walk around, and why should I come to a Serb town? I was arrested.."

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what exactly happened there?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: After we left Bosanski Samac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like -- this happened, I believe, in 1999, well after the indictment period or anything here. I'd like Mr. Lukic to explain how it can be relevant to her credibility issue. It was put in the statement as a matter of completion, but I don't see how it affects her credibility. I mean, it happened in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for me this is of extreme importance, because upon reading this, I, through my investigators, conducted some verifications and learned about what had actually happened there, and it has to do with the personality of this witness in that incident. It is very important for me to check out these allegations about what happened in 1999 and to confront the witness with information that I acquired. Perhaps I could go immediately to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you can be very brief, because a lot of time has passed and issues of credibility do also affect the time period when incidents which are being raised happened. Yes. We are discussing 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- Incidents here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but with Witness Lukac, we confronted him with an interview of -- he gave a year ago, and it had to do with his credibility. And this is something that applies to this witness as well. All I want to show is that this is a very confrontational person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, very briefly: On the 5th of July, 1999, in the premises of the police station in Pelagicevo and in the premises of the international police, did you attack the official policemen and tear official documents? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, in the presence of the representative of the international police, insult policemen who wanted to take you to a misdemeanor judge for disturbing public order? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No. Can you please allow me to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You could do that when the Prosecutor conducts the re-direct. Did you at that time state: "I am Bosnian and all of you will be Bosniaks in a year or else you will perish." Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, after that, go to the misdemeanour judge, or was there misdemeanour proceedings initiating due disturbance of public law and order

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a judicial warning issued to you after that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, after that, put up resistance to the Pelagicevo police and the international police?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No, I did not put up resistance. I didn't speak the language, and the gentlemen did what they wanted. I didn't speak the language and I couldn't explain in English to ask them what they wanted from me. They put handcuffs on me, and I have scars to this day. I also have doctors' reports concerning this. I simply wanted to go, to attend proceedings in Pelagicevo, where a document exempting or confiscating my property was discussed. That person who confiscated my property took it to his house, and my husband will bring this document to you. I had to go to Pelagicevo to meet the IPTF people and to state to them who confiscated my property. They gave me two policemen to escort me to go to this man's house so that he could say whether he confiscated our property and possibly returned it. In the meantime, they put handcuffs on my hands and they wouldn't let me move about as I wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, you said that you went to see the doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I hope had you have moved away from this topic, because one can see it was in the process of trying to recover her property, and obviously a lot of misunderstandings could have arisen, so that we don't need to go into this any further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't go on. I need a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all I'm trying to do is to clarify the purpose of my questions. I was unable to acquire these documents, but my investigator checked the record that exists in the Court. According to that court record, this witness stated or said to the policemen that they will see what kind of fate will befall them. It is very important for me to check the credibility of this witness, which I think is one of the basic rights pursuant to Rule 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but I think this particular event is too extraneous to the proceedings. And the witness said she needed a break. Maybe we can break for ten minutes. We'll rise for ten minutes to allow the witness to recover. --- Break taken at 1.07 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, I will put questions about the exchange, but before I do that, let me ask you something else relating to another incident and to your credibility. You can just give me a yes-or-no answer. Were you, Mrs. Bobic, convicted of the criminal offence of bodily injury because you wounded your brother's husband [As interpreted] with a knife in your kebab stand?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have information that that was in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, yes or no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: There's some confusion in transcript, because you wounded your brother's husband." Who was wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just clarify. There's a mistake in the transcript. I have information that this took place in 1987 and that this witness, Bobic, Ediba, wounded, in the stomach, her husband's brother, in her restaurant. So she was the perpetrator of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just reply with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, now that you are bringing this year up: This took place while we worked. We did not have an argument, and that did take place. We did not have an argument. I was simply there holding a knife, and then I suddenly turned around and that happened. I know why you are bringing this up. I'm not a criminal. I'm not a criminal of the type of those who are right here today, so don't bring this up. Let's analyse who did what, and if you are going to bring this up, then I will witnesses and papers. I am a witness here and I am testifying about things that you are asking about or the Judges are asking me about. I've answering questions from the 17th of April up until today, and not that happened a hundred years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me whether you were convicted criminally.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: No, I was not criminally convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we will turn to the exchange. You talked about that on two occasions today. Let us first clarify certain things regarding the time when you applied to be exchanged. You told us at the time that Mr. Tadic was in charge of the exchange. Do you remember where it was that people went to apply for the exchange?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I don't know where people went to apply. I was unable to apply to be exchanged. I had to look for Miro, Brko, in order to establish some contacts to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You claim that you did not apply with anybody to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I did apply. I did apply. But all of us had to personally beg Mr. Miro Brko to be exchanged. You are wrong, sir. You don't know what I experienced. All you know is what you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking the Judges to assist me. I'm putting very specific questions and I need a yes-or-no answer. Did you, madam, go to apply and put your name down with the Red Cross to be exchanged? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's all I care about. Please tell me: Where did you go? Where were the offices of the Red Cross? Where did you go to apply to put your name down?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: It was in the old hotel, upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, when you went to put your name down for exchange, you and your family and your son and your sister, with her family, that you had to give information of the person who was your guarantor? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember giving to the Red Cross information that your guarantor was Calic Zekija from Orasje, Omladinska Street?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Those were the exchanges in 1992. We are not allowed to leave in 1992, and it was my husband's sister asking that we be allowed to exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it was in 1992 when you applied to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but we didn't leave then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, you also put down your son and your sister and her family to be exchanged. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are not waiting for the interpretation to be completed after the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a document here which is a list of people who put their names down as those who want to cross to the opposing, enemy's side, in order to reunite families. This was the document that doesn't have any, and today we would just like to have the witness inspect this document, and we are not tendering it into evidence. And this document was disclosed to the Prosecution in 1998.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I put my name down in every single exchange, because I didn't want to remain there and live under very difficult circumstances. However, I did not manage to leave. It wasn't easy to leave. You couldn't just get into your car and go where you pleased. One had to break through that encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, your family from Orasje, namely, Zekija Calic, asked for you to be exchanged back in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you also described your conversation with Mr. Tadic. You also described it to the Prosecution twice. You said that the conversation took place in the municipal building. Do you remember whether Tadic had his office there, where Blagoje Simic sent you, or was he merely in somebody else's office?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I found him there, but I don't know whether the office was his.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it was on the same floor as the office of Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. But as we got upstairs, the doctor's office was on the left and Miro's office was on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he alone in the office or with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: He was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he sit at a desk or somewhere near the desk? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was at the desk. I walked in. He greeted me courteously. He was nice to me, and I talked to him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on your today's testimony, I took it that you went to see him the following day and gave him the money in that municipal building.

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was what we agreed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there somebody else there or were you alone?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you came to Dadic [phoen] all by yourself?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, can you describe how that all transpired?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't regret paying money just in order to be able to leave. My sister's baby was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to [Microphone not activated] I'm asking the witness just the facts about the meeting [Microphone not activated] I don't want anything about the family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. But don't keep interrupting the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you came on the 12th of December to the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me what exactly happened. How did you enter the building and so on?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: This is how it happened: I entered the building and some of our girls were waiting down there, and I asked them whether they had seen Vlajko, and they said no -- no, I apologise. I mean Miro Brko. Because I met Vlajko on my way there. So I went upstairs. There was nobody there. I entered the corridor. It was vacant too. I knocked on the door, and then Miro came into the corridor and told me that everything was fine. I gave him an envelope with money. He put it in his pocket without counting and left. And he told me everything would be okay and we would see each other at the exchange. He escorted me to the stairwell. I went down and he remained up there. I don't know whether he remembers that, but he should be able to remember that, because a number of us left at the -- at the time, but not my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, you said that Miro Tadic came out into the corridor and that you gave him money there?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was anyone sitting in his office?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see that the office was empty at the time when you got in?

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I didn't get in at all. I opened the door. He was there. He quickly got out and did that. He took the money and said that we would be exchanged. I didn't think about the money at all. I didn't think about anything. I was just thinking about how happy I was to leave, how happy I would be when I would be able to sleep quietly in a peaceful land.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bobic, in May this year, in paragraph 72, you stated the following: "I took all 12.000 German marks to him. I had money hidden where they couldn't find it."

utterances.speaker: EDIBA BOBIC
